title: How to set up Salesforce authentication to access any Docusign API
summary: Learn to configure your authentication in Salesforce so you can call any Docusign API from an Apex class.
body_markdown:
Integrating Docusign eSignature with Salesforce has historically been made easy with the help of the[Apex Toolkit](https://developers.docusign.com/docs/salesforce/) . With the introduction of Docusign IAM, the[Salesforce extension app](https://apps.docusign.com/app-center/app/2d576583-520a-41e2-886b-089fefe733a1) has made it frictionless to bring Salesforce into your[Docusign workflows](https://support.docusign.com/s/document-item?bundleId=yff1696971835267&topicId=dnx1696972415150.html) to automate agreement processes. But with the wide variety of[Docusign APIs](https://developers.docusign.com/docs/) and Salesforce’s breadth of configuration options, there are so many more possibilities for what you can build beyond what’s available out-of-the-box.


For example, you might call the[Agreement Manager API](https://developers.docusign.com/docs/navigator-api/) from Agentforce to access data from a smart agreement repository. Or you might build a button that calls the[Workflow Builder API](https://developers.docusign.com/docs/maestro-api/) , triggering custom extensible workflows from inside Salesforce. While authentication for eSignature is made simple with the Apex Toolkit, other APIs that aren’t included in[eSignature for Salesforce opens in a new tab](https://appexchange.salesforce.com/appxListingDetail?listingId=a0N30000001taX4EAI) require a different method of authentication before you can take advantage of their unique capabilities.


In this post, I’m going to walk you through how to authenticate with[JSON Web Token (JWT)](https://developers.docusign.com/platform/auth/jwt/) so you can call any Docusign API from an Apex class in Salesforce.


**What is JWT Grant authentication?** JWT Grant is an OAuth 2.0 flow that allows server-to-server authentication without user interaction by using a cryptographically signed token. This approach is ideal for automated integrations and background processes where no user is present to authorize access.


**When to use this approach:** JWT authentication via named credentials is specifically designed for Docusign APIs not covered by the Apex Toolkit, such as the Agreement Manager API or Workflow Builder API. If you're working exclusively with eSignature, the Apex Toolkit provides a simpler authentication path.


## Prerequisites


Before you begin, ensure you have the following:


-


A[Docusign developer account](https://www.docusign.com/developers/sandbox)


-


A Salesforce org with administrator access


-


[OpenSSL opens in a new tab](https://docs.openssl.org/master/) installed on your local machine


-


An integration key created in Docusign with an RSA key pair


## Authentication with named credentials


To make raw HTTP requests from an Apex class, you first need to authenticate with the Agreement Manager API. The easiest way to do this in Salesforce is through[named credentials opens in a new tab](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.named_credentials_about.htm&type=5) .


**Configuration steps overview:**


1.


Upload your private key as certificate


2.


Create an authentication provider


3.


Grant consent


4.


Create an external credential


5.


Create a named credential


6.


Assign the external credential to a permission set


I’m going to walk through the steps required to set up a named credential in this post, but if you’d prefer to watch a video demonstration, see Steven Cooke’s **Named Credentials** video:


### Upload your private key as a certificate in Salesforce


First, create a new[integration key](https://developers.docusign.com/platform/configure-app/) in your Docusign developer account. Add an[RSA key pair](https://developers.docusign.com/platform/configure-app/#rsa-key-pair) to your app and save the private key in a file with the extension .key on your local desktop. Now the .key file needs to be converted to a format that can be uploaded to Salesforce as a Signing Certificate. You can accomplish this by running the following commands in the command line of your choice.


1.


Convert the .key file to a .pem file. Replace <file-name> with the name of the file where you stored your private key. Replace <certificate-name> with the name of the new file where the output of this command will be stored.` openssl req -new -x509 -key <file-name>.key -out <certificate-name>.pem -days 1095`


2.


Create a .p12 file from the .pem and .key files. You will be prompted to create a password for the certificate.` openssl pkcs12 -export -in <certificate-name>.pem -inkey <file-name>.key -certfile <certificate-name>.pem -out <certificate-name>.p12`


3.


Create a .jks file from the .p12 file. You will again be prompted to create a password. Be sure to use the same password that you used in the previous command. Salesforce will not let you upload the certificate if the passwords don’t match.` keytool -importkeystore -srckeystore <certificate-name>.p12 -srcstoretype pkcs12 -destkeystore <certificate-name>.jks -deststoretype JKS`


4.


Give the key an[alias opens in a new tab](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000387657&type=1) that will be accepted by Salesforce.` keytool -keystore <certificate-name>.jks -changealias -alias 1 -destalias docusignjwt` Now your private key has been stored in a format that can be uploaded as a certificate to Salesforce.


5.


In **Salesforce Setup** , navigate to **Certificate and Key Management** .


6.


Before you can upload your Docusign certificate, Salesforce requires that you complete two prerequisites, including creating a Self-Signed certificate in your account and enabling[Identity Provider opens in a new tab](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.identity_provider_enable.htm&type=5) . To create the certificate, choose **Create Self-Signed Certificate** and give it a name and label. Then, enable Identity Provider and assign this new self-signed certificate as the chosen certificate.


7.


Once those prerequisites have been completed, you can return to **Certificate and Key Management** and choose **Import from Keystore** . Upload the .jks file created in the previous steps and enter the password that you used when creating that file.


### Create an authentication provider for Docusign


In **Salesforce Setup** , navigate to **Auth. Providers** . Select **New** , then choose Open ID Connect for the Provider Type. Configure the Auth. Provider with the following fields:


-


**Consumer Key:** Enter the value of the integration key where you created the RSA keypair in the previous steps


-


**Consumer Secret:** Add a[secret key](https://developers.docusign.com/platform/configure-app/#secret-key) to your integration key and copy that value here


-


**Authorize Endpoint URL:** https://account-d.docusign.com/oauth/auth


-


**Token Endpoint URL:** https://account-d.docusign.com/oauth/token


-


**Use Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) Extension:** Uncheck this box


-


**Default Scopes:** This should include all of the[scopes](https://developers.docusign.com/platform/auth/reference/scopes/) that you need for the API of your choice and an additional scope openid. For example, if you were authenticating with the[Agreement Manager API](https://developers.docusign.com/docs/navigator-api/) you would enter the following:` signature adm_store_unified_repo_read impersonation openid`


-


**Send access token in header:** Check this box


-


**Include Consumer Secret in SOAP API Responses:** Check this box


This screenshot shows an example of an Auth. Provider configured with these fields.


After saving your Auth. Provider, you should see a few URLs that were automatically generated for you at the bottom of the page, similar to those in the screenshot below.


Add the OAuth-Only Initialization URL and Callback URL as[redirect URIs](https://developers.docusign.com/platform/configure-app/#redirect-uri) in your integration key.


### Grant consent


To grant consent, copy the OAuth-Only Initialization URL into a new browser tab. This will redirect you to the consent flow pictured below. After granting consent, you’ll be redirected back to Salesforce.


### Create an external credential


In **Salesforce Setup** , navigate to **Named Credentials** , then choose the **External Credentials** tab. Select **New** . Select **OAuth 2.0** for the Authentication Protocol and **JWT Bearer Flow** for the Authentication Flow Type. Set the identity provider URL to **https://account-d.docusign.com/oauth/token.** Set the JWT Expiration to **3600.**


After saving that, scroll to **JWT Claims** and choose **Edit** . Set the values of the claims following the table below:


**Claim Name**


**Value**


**Description**


iss


The value of your integration key


Issuer - identifies the application making the request


sub


The user ID of your Docusign account


Subject - the user being impersonated


aud


account-d.docusign.com


Audience - the authorization server


scope


Any scopes required to make the API calls, separated by spaces. In this example use the following:


adm_store_unified_repo_read signature impersonation


Requested permissions for the token


After updating these values, the JWT Claims on your external credential should look similar to this screenshot:


Finally, add a principal to the external credential by scrolling to **Principals** and selecting **New** . Give the principal a name and choose **Named Principal** for the Identity Type.


### Create a named credential


Navigate to **Named Credentials** and choose the **Named Credentials** tab. Select **New** . Give the credential a descriptive label and name. Set URL to the base path for the Agreement Manager API: https://api-d.docusign.com/v1. For the associated External Credential, choose the external credential that you created in the previous step. After saving this, your named credential and external credential will be linked.


### Assign the external credential to a permission set


In **Salesforce Setup** , navigate to **Permission Sets** , and create a new permission. Edit that permission set, and from the edit view, choose **External Credential Principal Access** .


Select **Edit** , then select the external credential that you just created and use the arrow buttons to add that to the box labeled **Enabled External Credential Principals** . Then click **Save** .


Finally, be sure that this permission set is assigned to the user who will be making the API calls.


Now you’re ready to call the API of your choice. In your code, use callout:{YOUR_NAMED_CREDENTIAL_NAME} in place of the endpoint’s base path. The snippet below shows what this looks like.


` req.setEndpoint('callout:AgreementManager/accounts/{API_ACCOUNT_ID}/agreements');`


With this authentication through named credentials, you can call any Docusign API from inside an Apex class, allowing you to bring even more Docusign functionality into Salesforce. When developing with Salesforce and the eSignature REST API, we recommend using the[Apex Toolkit](https://developers.docusign.com/docs/salesforce/) , but with named credentials, you can go beyond eSignature, leveraging a wide variety of other Docusign features.


## Troubleshooting common issues


If you encounter issues during setup, check for these common problems:


-


**Certificate password mismatch** : Ensure you use the same password when creating the .p12 and .jks files. Salesforce will reject the certificate if passwords don't match.


-


**Consent not granted** : If API calls fail with authorization errors, verify you completed the consent flow by visiting the OAuth-Only Initialization URL.


-


**Incorrect scopes** : Ensure your scopes match the API you're calling. Missing the impersonation scope is a common oversight for JWT flows.


**Token endpoint failures** : Verify the identity provider URL is set correctly to https://account-d.docusign.com/oauth/token for the demo environment.
